comparison: Perfect alignment on computational-experimental integration (C83-95). Both recognize the CpHMD refinement using MST data and the thermodynamic modeling as important contributions. Peer review explicitly states this 'constitutes an important contribution' while OpenEval notes the approach is 'methodologically sound' despite initial prediction limitations.

Perfect alignment on the two-step Zn2+ binding mechanism (C119-123). Both accept the proposed mechanism involving initial binding to low-affinity site B followed by migration to high-affinity site A. However, OpenEval rates this as UNCERTAIN due to speculative nature, while peer reviewers accept it as SUPPORTED within the proposed transport cycle.

Perfect alignment on broader implications for CDF family (C145-148). Both accept the extrapolation to other CDF members and eukaryotic systems. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to speculative nature beyond experimental system, while peer review explicitly endorses this as 'basis for future work on other systems such as human ZnT transporters.'

Strong alignment on domain-swapping and site C's role in dimer stability (C59-72). Both accept the structural characterization and SEC analysis. OpenEval notes C82 suggests Fab-induced domain swap limits physiological interpretation, while peer reviewers accept these findings as supporting dimer integrity without expressing concern about Fab effects.

Strong alignment on pH-dependent binding affinity at each site (C73-79). Both accept the MST experimental data showing dramatic pH dependence at site A and more modest changes at sites B and C. Peer review emphasizes the MST analysis 'further clarified the pH dependence' while OpenEval notes data is 'internally consistent and appropriately quantified.'

Partial alignment on stoichiometry determination (C10-11, C130-132). Both accept the 1:2-3 Zn2+:H+ stoichiometry from MST inference modeling. Peer review (R8) focuses on stoichiometry prediction while OpenEval (R5) emphasizes the integration of experimental MST data with thermodynamic modeling. Peer R12 also addresses thermodynamic implications (C137-141).

Strong alignment on thermodynamic and kinetic implications (C137-144). Both accept the energetic coupling of Zn2+ export to proton-motive force and the kinetic consequences of differential binding affinities. Peer review emphasizes this addresses 'energetic coupling' while OpenEval notes the inference about differential rates is 'thermodynamically sound.'

Strong alignment on D51A mutant structural validation (C30-34). Both accept the cryo-EM structure confirms intended mutation effect with minimal overall perturbation. Peer review notes 'high-quality 3D structural determination' while OpenEval emphasizes the presence of density at sites B and C as internal control confirming specificity.

Partial alignment on mutant structural characterization (C35-39). OpenEval focuses on structural validation and comparison with published structure, while peer review (R2) addresses the broader set of mutant structures. Both accept the structural data quality without question.

Strong alignment on site B's role in conformational transitions (C40-46). Both accept the D70A mutant cryo-EM structures showing conformational changes and site A occlusion. Peer review emphasizes 'distinct structural/functional roles' while OpenEval notes 'convergence of experimental structures and computational predictions strongly supports this mechanism.'

Partial alignment on MD simulations and structural dynamics (C50-58). Both accept MD simulations confirming increased loop mobility and structural changes. Peer review acknowledges MD as part of comprehensive approach while OpenEval emphasizes how simulations confirm experimental observations about site B's role.

Partial alignment on core findings about three binding sites (C6-7). OpenEval groups site C dimer stabilization evidence while peer review addresses all three sites' roles together. Both strongly support the findings but organize the evidence differently - peer review emphasizes the overall 'thermodynamic landscape' while OpenEval focuses on specific structural evidence for site C.

Strong alignment on site C's role and TMD-CTD interactions (C101-105). Both accept the comparison of binding affinities between full-length and isolated CTDs supporting TMD's role in enhancing CTD stability. Peer review emphasizes 'integrity of homodimeric structure' while OpenEval focuses on reconciling isolated domain observations with full-length behavior.

Partial alignment on TMD interface conservation (C99-100). Both accept that TMD interface is conserved despite CTD conformational changes, ruling out scissoring movements. Peer review addresses this within broader discussion of dimer integrity while OpenEval emphasizes the mechanistic conclusion about transport mechanism.

Partial alignment on general CDF structural principles (C96-98). Both accept established CDF structural features as appropriate background. Peer review treats these as accepted context while OpenEval uses them to support mechanistic conclusions about YiiP specifically.

Strong alignment on background and context (C1-5). Both accept these as well-established facts from prior literature providing necessary background. Peer review confirms YiiP as 'widely used model system' while OpenEval notes these are 'appropriately cited and providing necessary background for the study.'

Perfect alignment on theoretical basis for pKa shifts (C135-136). Both accept cited precedents for significant pKa shifts in metal-binding proteins as supporting the plausibility of predicted shifts. Neither questions the magnitude of shifts observed in the modeling.

Partial alignment on pKa shift predictions (C133-134). Both accept the thermodynamic modeling predicting significant pKa shifts. Peer review accepts the detailed per-site overview while OpenEval emphasizes the mechanistic explanation is sound and supported by cited prior work.

Strong alignment on cooperative binding at site C (C75-76, C80). Both accept MST experiments with site-specific mutants demonstrating cooperativity through reduced affinity when sites are isolated and high Hill coefficient. OpenEval notes variability in Hill coefficients introduces some uncertainty while peer review accepts the findings without reservation.

Strong alignment on MST experimental controls (C81-82). Both accept SEC analysis demonstrating mutations don't disrupt native structure absent Fab, supporting inference that Fab induces domain swap. This is important for interpreting physiological relevance of D287A/H263A structure.

Strong alignment on asymmetric protomer function (C117-118). Both accept the D70A_asym structure demonstrates independent protomer function. Peer review calls this 'another nice achievement' confirming previous suggestions, while OpenEval notes this has 'important implications for the transport mechanism.'

Alignment on sequential conformational pathway with different confidence levels (C110-111). Both address the proposed sequential pathway from structural observations. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN noting explicit speculation, while peer review accepts this as part of the 'compelling' support for the transport cycle.

Partial alignment on structural basis of occlusion and energetics (C114-116). Both accept structural observations about occlusion mechanism. OpenEval notes some aspects are speculative but overall reasonable, while peer review accepts these as part of the mechanistic model without expressing uncertainty.

Partial alignment on electrostatic changes and conformational transitions (C57-58). Both accept structural analysis showing electrostatic consequences of conformational changes. Peer review acknowledges this as part of comprehensive structural approach while OpenEval emphasizes the mechanistic explanation for directional ion movement.

Partial alignment on site A occlusion mechanism (C112-113). Both accept the structural basis for occlusion and its electrostatic consequences. Peer review addresses this within the broader transport cycle while OpenEval focuses on the specific structural and electrostatic documentation.

Strong alignment on mutagenesis strategy (C27-29). Both accept the approach of generating mutants to abolish specific Zn2+ binding sites for structural and functional characterization. Peer review confirms mutants 'removed one or two of the three zinc(II) binding sites' while OpenEval validates the strategy with structural confirmation.

Partial alignment on SEC analysis and oligomerization (C62, C68-69). Both accept SEC data supporting conclusions about site C's role. OpenEval emphasizes SEC confirms oligomeric state in domain-swapped complex, while peer review addresses this within broader discussion of dimer integrity.
